Chronology 2 — The Fall and the Origin of Sin

This is the single most consequential divergence in the whole study: the same garden scene yields opposite anthropologies, and from that fork everything downstream (atonement, the cross, salvation at the end) follows by logical necessity.

The Bible's text — what is actually said

  • The act: the serpent's "you will be like God" (Gen 3:5); they eat.
  • God's words: "Where are you?" (3:9) — the summons; then the interrogation, the man blaming the woman, the woman blaming the serpent.
  • The curses (3:14–19): the serpent, the pain of childbirth, the cursed ground, "dust you are, and to dust you shall return."
  • *Gen 3:15 — the protoevangelium: "he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel" — read by Christians, retrospectively, as the first thread of redemption. (By the dossier's symmetry rule this retrospective reading is flagged exactly like "Let Us make man" in cap. 10: suggestive within the cumulative case, not a stand-alone proof.)*
  • Expulsion: driven out, the cherubim and flaming sword guard the tree of life (3:24) — access to life is now barred.
  • The doctrine that grows from it: "through one man sin entered… death spread to all" (Rom 5:12–19); "in sin did my mother conceive me" (Ps 51:5). This was sharpened by Augustine vs. Pelagius (5th c.) into Western original sin. Note the internal Christian split: Eastern Orthodoxy teaches ancestral sin — inherited mortality and corruption, not inherited personal guilt — which is materially closer to the Islamic objection than the Augustinian/Reformed form.
  • Eve is "deceived" first (1 Tim 2:14); Adam's act is the federal one (Rom 5 makes Adam, not Eve, the head).

The Qur'an's text — what is actually said

  • Both Adam and his spouse are tempted by Iblis/Shaytan, both eat (Q 7:19–25; 20:120–122); blame is shared, with no "Eve caused it" framing.
  • Their confession is the model penitent prayer: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves; if You do not forgive us… we will be among the losers" (Q 7:23) — they own it, blaming no one.
  • Satan's vow sets up earthly life as a moral test: "I will surely lead them astray…" (Q 7:16–17; 15:39; 38:82); "Descend, as enemies to one another" (Q 2:36).
  • Forgiven on the spot: "Then Adam received words from his Lord, and He accepted his repentance" (Q 2:37); "then his Lord chose him, turned to him, and guided" (Q 20:122).
  • No original sin, no inherited guilt: "no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another" (Q 35:18; 6:164; 53:38). Each soul is born in fiṭra and answers only for its own deeds. (Tradition even makes Adam a prophet, raising the 'isma question — flagged as tradition, not Qurʾanic text.)
  • The descent is within the announced plan — Adam as khalifa (Q 2:30).

Collision

QuestionBibleQur'an
Is guilt inherited?Yes (original sin)No (Q 35:18)
Is human nature corrupted by the Fall?YesNo (fitra intact)
Was the first sin immediately forgiven?No — sets up redemptionYes (Q 2:37)
Is a redeemer therefore required?YesNo
Is Eve singled out?Comparatively yesNo — shared

This is not an emphasis difference. It is a binary fork. Original sin is the reason Christianity needs a cross; its absence is why Islam needs none — exactly the forgiveness-mechanism split already isolated in cap. 09 §2.4.

The Bible against itself — Ezekiel 18

Symmetry demands a point that helps the Muslim case and must therefore be stated plainly: the Bible itself contains Q 35:18's principle.

"The soul that sins shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father the iniquity of the son" (Ezek 18:20; cf. Deut 24:16; Jer 31:30).

So "no one bears another's burden" is not unique to the Qur'an — it is also biblical, and it sits in internal tension with Rom 5's inherited death. Christian theology reconciles this by distinguishing inherited corruption/mortality (a condition, transmitted) from personal guilt (a verdict, not transferred) — and via federal headship (Adam and Christ as covenant representatives, Rom 5:12–21). Whether that reconciliation is convincing is contestable; that the tension is internal to the Bible is simply true, and pretending otherwise would breach the symmetry rule (Methodology §3).

The textual bridge — Adam to Christ

The load-bearing verses that make the cross necessary in the Christian system are explicit and must be named:

"As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive" (1 Cor 15:22); "as by one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by one man's obedience the many will be made righteous" (Rom 5:19).

This Adam–Christ typology is the hinge of the entire seam: the Fall creates the deficit; the cross (cap. 16) pays it; the verdict at the end (cap. 18) applies it. Remove inherited death and the bridge has nothing to span — which is precisely the Islamic position.

Logic

  • "No one bears another's burden" is a clean ethical axiom and — per Ezek 18 — is affirmed by both scriptures. The Muslim cannot claim it as a Qurʾan-only insight; the Christian cannot deny it is biblical.
  • The genuine divergence is narrower than usually stated: not "is transferred guilt just?" (both texts say no), but "is human nature itself inherited-corrupt, requiring a redeemer?" Bible: yes (Rom 5, federal headship). Qurʾan: no (fiṭra intact, Q 2:37 closes the matter).
  • The Christian model has explanatory power for the empirically universal fact of wrongdoing; the Qurʾanic model has ethical cleanliness and needs no atonement apparatus. Each answers a different question and is internally coherent.

Arbiter verdict — the Fall

Present. Same narrative skeleton (couple, tempter, transgression, consequence); opposite doctrines of what it did to humanity.

Weigh.

  • Symmetric correction: the "no one bears another's burden" principle is biblical too (Ezek 18:20) — so it is not a clean Qurʾan-vs-Bible win; it is, in part, a Bible-internal tension.
  • Strong (Islam, textual + ethical): immediate forgiveness (Q 2:37) and fiṭra are explicit; no atonement apparatus is needed.
  • Strong (Christianity, explanatory + textual): the Adam–Christ bridge (Rom 5; 1 Cor 15) is explicit and gives the system its reason for the cross; original sin (esp. the Orthodox corruption-not-guilt form) answers the universality of wrongdoing.
  • Decisive structural fact: this fork necessitates every later divergence about atonement and salvation — the headwater of the seam.

Judge. The popular framing ("the Bible unjustly transfers guilt; the Qurʾan does not") is too crude and partly false: both texts reject transferred personal guilt (Ezek 18 = Q 35:18). The real, narrower divergence is inherited corruption requiring a redeemer (Bible) vs. an intact nature needing none (Qurʾan). On ethical parsimony: advantage Qurʾan — fewer moving parts, and its principle is even conceded by the Bible. On explanatory scope and textual integration: advantage Bible — the Adam–Christ typology is explicit and load- bearing. Which a true revelation should prioritise — a clean ethic or an explanation of universal sin — is the non-arbitrable value premise (Methodology §5). Not in doubt: from here the two systems are logically committed to diverge all the way to the end.
